title: Bone marrow failure and aplastic anemia
covers: Acquired and inherited bone marrow failure: aplastic anemia (causes, overlap with PNH and MDS, workup, severity grades, treatment), the inherited syndromes (Fanconi, dyskeratosis congenita, Shwachman-Diamond, CAT, Diamond-Blackfan, CDA, SCN, TAR) and the differential of pancytopenia.

table: Anemia + leukopenia + thrombocytopenia; a finding, not a diagnosis
Hypo/acellular marrow from loss of stem and progenitor cells, with pancytopenia and low reticulocytes
The marrow cannot make enough blood cells; many causes, including AA

ul: BMF predisposes to clonal neoplasms: AML, MDS, PNH, LGL leukemia.
Acquired BMF is more frequent than inherited. Telling them apart matters: it changes therapy and prognosis.
Three age peaks: 2–5 years (mostly inherited), 20–25 years, above 65 years (mostly acquired).

table: Leukemia, lymphoma, myeloma, myelofibrosis, storage disorders, sarcoidosis, amyloidosis
Fanconi anemia, dyskeratosis congenita, Shwachman-Diamond, congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia
Diamond-Blackfan anemia, congenital dyserythropoietic anemia, severe congenital neutropenia, TAR

ul: The commonest BMF syndrome; rare (2–4 per million per year); both sexes equally. 5-year survival up to 80% with modern therapy; high mortality untreated.
Three routes end in the same empty marrow: physical/chemical damage, immune destruction, constitutional genetic defect.
Immune (most severe and acute cases): T cells destroy stem and progenitor cells. Single-lineage cytopenias (ITP, AIHA) are antibody-mediated instead.

Viruses: hepatitis, HIV, CMV, EBV, parvovirus. Hepatitis and HIV are linked to severe AA. Mostly immune: activated T cells release cytokines, and a cytotoxic clone recognizes similar antigens on liver and marrow cells. Parvovirus B19 infects progenitors directly.
Drugs (antibiotics, chemotherapy, antiseizure and antithyroid drugs, NSAIDs): idiosyncratic or dose-dependent. Idiosyncratic reactions (chloramphenicol) can leave irreversible AA.
Ionizing radiation: predictable, dose-dependent. Toxins (benzene, industrial chemicals, insecticides, pesticides): severe AA.
Inherited BMF syndromes (below).

items.note: Slide 11 lists hepatitis A, B, C and D. Standard sources say hepatitis-associated aplastic anemia usually follows seronegative (non-A to E) hepatitis. Only "hepatitis" was tested. Slide 8 gives AA peaks in "mid-late childhood and elderly" and clonal evolution in about 1/3; standard sources put the peaks in adolescents/young adults and older adults. Neither was tested.

items.p: AA can coexist with or evolve into PNH, MDS, AML or LGL leukemia, an inherited BMF syndrome, or other autoimmune disease.

table: Acquired stem cell disorder; PIGA mutation → no CD59 (intravascular hemolysis) or CD55 (extravascular hemolysis). Hemolysis, thrombosis, dark urine, end-organ damage; anemia ± low WBC and platelets. De novo or with AA, MDS, PMF. Treatment: eculizumab.

Most common acquired marrow disorder in adults. Clonal; cytopenia, ineffective hematopoiesis, AML in high-risk cases. Hypercellular dysplastic marrow, blasts usually < 20%, ringed sideroblasts. Hypoplastic MDS mimics AA.
Clonal adult disease: cytopenia, splenomegaly, LGLs in blood and marrow

ul: Clinical: pallor, bleeding, fatigue, recurrent infections. CBC: pancytopenia, low reticulocytes.
Marrow aspirate and biopsy: hypocellular, empty fatty marrow, no malignant cells or fibrosis, CD34 cells almost absent.
Differential: infiltrative disease (leukemia, LGL leukemia, myelofibrosis), hypoplastic MDS, PNH, inherited BMF, megaloblastic anemia, hypersplenism, transient suppression.

items.p: A patient with SAA can have an unrecognized inherited BMF syndrome.
Choice depends on severity, age, donor availability and access; managed by an interprofessional team.

table: First-line SAA in children and young adults with a full match; high cure. Survival ~86% at 1–20 years, 76% at 21–40, 55% over 40.
New SAA/VSAA over 40 years; younger patients without a matched sibling
New SAA/VSAA with inadequate IST response who cannot have BMT; works better combined with IST
Treat and prevent infections, restrictive transfusions, iron chelation, G-CSF in fever and neutropenia, remove the cause

ul: SAA survival rose from ~30% (1960) to ~85% (2018): more HSCT, better IST, targeted therapy, better supportive care.
SAA/VSAA mortality is > 70% with supportive care alone.
BMF + congenital/developmental abnormalities + cancer predisposition; germline or new mutations.
Clues: young onset (can appear in adults), family history, chronic course, several organs involved, high HbF and MCV.

table: Early onset, family history, consanguinity, chronic cytopenia
Congenital anomalies, short stature, early greying
Raised HbF, positive DEB test, very short telomeres

items.p: Lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly with pancytopenia → malignancy.

table: Skin pigmentation 60%, short stature 57%, upper limb/thumb 48%, microcephaly, renal; 20% look normal; onset 3–12 years
Chromosome breakage (radials) with DEB or mitomycin C
Telomere biology (X-linked DKC1 most severe; also AD and AR)
Skin pigmentation, nail dystrophy, oral leukoplakia (often absent early); BMF in 85% and the main cause of death; lung/liver fibrosis
Pancreatic insufficiency, malabsorption, infections, neutropenia, short stature, skeletal anomalies, AML/MDS risk
Early thrombocytopenia, few megakaryocytes, no birth defects; may evolve to AA, MDS, AML

items.p: Breakage test: in infants with thumb/arm anomalies and in AA at any age before HSCT.

items.note: Slide 35 gives X-linked DC as 80% of cases; slide 46 lists abnormal neutrophil chemotaxis under DC, while slide 36 gives it to Shwachman-Diamond; slide 36 says SBDS mutations are found in up to 75%. These details were not tested.

table: Early pure red cell aplasia; craniofacial, skeletal (thumb), cardiac, urogenital anomalies
Isolated macrocytic anemia, reticulocytopenia, few red cell precursors, high HbF and red cell ADA
Anemia, jaundice, gallstones, splenomegaly, iron overload
Ineffective erythropoiesis, erythroblast nuclear abnormalities, genotyping
Early thrombocytopenia, absent radii, cardiac, skeletal, urogenital anomalies; uncertain cancer risk

items.note: Slide 42 says "absent 1 or 2 radii"; TAR is classically bilateral. Not tested.

ul: Supportive care as in AA, plus pancreatic enzymes in Shwachman-Diamond, androgens, and splenectomy/cholecystectomy in CDA.

Stem cell transplant: curative for the cytopenia in 60–90%, but does not lower the early cancer risk. Not recommended in DC (interstitial lung disease). Gene therapy is emerging. Monitor organs and cancer.
Prognosis by cause: inherited = lifelong cytopenia and higher cancer risk; acquired = short course but can be permanent and life-threatening; viral = usually self-limiting.
Main causes of morbidity and death: infection, bleeding, BMT complications, second cancers.
Adults with AA: look for MDS, PNH and AML in all; test genetically for inherited disease and when IST fails. Children: genetic testing.

table: Infiltrative marrow disease (cancer, myelofibrosis, TB, fungi, storage cells)
Blasts, schistocytes, teardrops on the smear; abnormal marrow
Oval macrocytes, hypersegmented neutrophils, high LDH and indirect bilirubin
Transient suppression (chemotherapy, radiation, sepsis, viral infection)
Predictable; serial CBCs improve in days to weeks
Hypersplenism (cirrhosis, portal vein thrombosis, infiltration, hemoglobinopathies)
Milder cytopenia; normal or increased marrow hematopoiesis

cards.q: Pancytopenia versus aplastic anemia versus bone marrow failure
cards.a: Pancytopenia: CBC finding. AA: marrow finding (empty marrow). BMF: the syndrome, with many causes.

cards.q: Three age peaks of bone marrow failure
cards.a: 2–5 years (mostly inherited), 20–25 years, above 65 years (mostly acquired)
Aplastic anemia, MDS, PNH

cards.q: Mechanism of most severe acute aplastic anemia
cards.a: T cell-mediated destruction of stem and progenitor cells (single-lineage cytopenias are antibody-mediated)

cards.q: How do viruses cause aplastic anemia?
cards.a: Mostly immune (cytokines; a T cell clone hitting liver and marrow); parvovirus B19 infects progenitors directly
Chloramphenicol: idiosyncratic, can be irreversible. Radiation: predictable, dose-dependent.
PIGA; no CD59 (intravascular hemolysis) or CD55 (extravascular); eculizumab
MDS: hypercellular, dysplastic, blasts < 20%, ringed sideroblasts. AA: empty, fatty, CD34 cells absent.
Cellularity < 25% + 2 of: ANC < 0.5, platelets < 20, reticulocytes < 60 ×10⁹/L
SAA criteria + ANC < 0.2 ×10⁹/L

cards.q: First-line treatment of SAA by patient
cards.a: Young with matched sibling: BMT. Over 40, or no sibling donor: ATG + cyclosporine.
Thrombopoietin receptor agonist; inadequate IST response and no BMT; better with IST
Infection care, restrictive transfusions, iron chelation, G-CSF in febrile neutropenia, remove the cause

cards.q: SAA mortality with supportive care alone
Clues to an inherited BMF syndrome
cards.a: Young onset, family history, chronicity, multi-organ involvement, high HbF and MCV
Sudden severe pancytopenia, previously normal counts, preceding hepatitis, PNH clone

cards.q: What must every adult with AA be checked for?
cards.a: Coexisting MDS, PNH and AML
AR DNA repair defect; most common IBMFS; skin pigmentation, short stature, thumb/arm anomalies (20% look normal); DEB breakage test

cards.q: When is the chromosome breakage test done?
cards.a: Infants with thumb/arm anomalies; AA at any age before HSCT
Telomere disease; skin pigmentation, nail dystrophy, oral leukoplakia; X-linked DKC1 most severe; BMF main cause of death; no SCT (lung disease)
AR ribosome (SBDS) disease; pancreatic insufficiency, neutropenia, short stature; pancreatic enzymes
MPL (TPO receptor); early thrombocytopenia, few megakaryocytes, no birth defects
Pure red cell aplasia, RPS19, mostly AD; macrocytic anemia, high HbF and red cell ADA; thumb and other anomalies
Ineffective erythropoiesis, erythroblast nuclear abnormalities; jaundice, gallstones, splenomegaly, iron overload; splenectomy/cholecystectomy
AR, RBM8A; early thrombocytopenia with absent radii

cards.q: What does SCT not fix in inherited BMF?
cards.a: The early cancer risk (cytopenia cured in 60–90%)
Blasts, schistocytes, teardrop cells
Hypersplenism: normal or increased hematopoiesis. AA: empty fatty marrow.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old's CBC shows anemia, leukopenia and thrombocytopenia. Nothing else is known yet. What has been established?
questions.explanation: Pancytopenia (anemia + leukopenia + thrombocytopenia) is a CBC finding, not a diagnosis. Aplastic anemia is a marrow finding; BMF has many causes, including AA. B: Needs a marrow biopsy. C: Needs the cause established. D: Needs blasts. E: Needs splenomegaly.

questions.stem: Aplastic anemia is defined by the findings of which test?
questions.explanation: AA is a marrow finding: a hypo/acellular marrow from loss of HSPCs, with pancytopenia and a low reticulocyte count. A: Shows pancytopenia only. C: Low but not defining. D: Not defining. E: PNH.

questions.stem: Patients with bone marrow failure are predisposed to which disorder?
questions.explanation: BMF: failure of the marrow to produce enough blood cells, with predisposition to clonal neoplasms (AML, MDS, PNH, LGL leukemia). A: Inherited membrane defect. B: Inherited coagulation defect. D: Nutritional. E: Inherited globin defect.

questions.stem: In which patient with new bone marrow failure is an acquired cause most likely?
questions.explanation: BMF has 3 age peaks: 2–5 years (mostly inherited), 20–25 years, and above 65 years (mostly acquired). Acquired BMF is more frequent. A: The 2–5-year peak is mostly inherited. B: The 2–5-year peak is mostly inherited. C: Congenital anomalies point to inherited disease. D: Pancreatic insufficiency points to SDS.

questions.stem: Why must inherited and acquired bone marrow failure be told apart early?

options.C: It changes the CBC reference range

questions.explanation: Distinguishing inherited from acquired BMF is critical because it affects the choice of therapy and the prognosis. A: Not the reason given. B: Both need a marrow biopsy. C: Not the reason given. E: Not the reason given.

questions.stem: Bone marrow failure has three age peaks. Which peak is mostly due to inherited disease?
questions.explanation: Age peaks: 2–5 years (mostly inherited), 20–25 years, above 65 years (mostly acquired). A: Mixed. B: Mostly acquired. D: Not a peak. E: Not a peak.

questions.stem: Which is an acquired non-infiltrative cause of bone marrow failure?

options.C: Multiple myeloma with marrow plasma cells

questions.explanation: Acquired BMF: infiltrative (leukemia, lymphoma, myeloma, myelofibrosis, storage disorders, sarcoidosis, amyloidosis) or non-infiltrative (aplastic anemia, MDS, PNH). A: Infiltrative. C: Infiltrative. D: Infiltrative. E: Inherited.

questions.stem: Which inherited marrow failure syndrome affects a single cell line?
questions.explanation: Multiple cell lines: FA, DC, SDS, CAT. Single cell line: DBA, CDA, SCN, TAR. B: Multiple lines. C: Multiple lines. D: Multiple lines. E: Grouped with multiple lines.

questions.stem: With modern therapy, 5-year survival in aplastic anemia reaches about what level?
questions.explanation: AA: rare (2–4/million/year), both sexes equally; 5-year survival up to 80% with modern therapy; high mortality if untreated. A: Survival around 1960. B: Too low. C: Too low. D: Too high.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old with very severe aplastic anemia declines transplant and immunosuppression and receives transfusions only. What outcome is expected?
questions.explanation: SAA and VSAA: mortality rate > 70% with supportive care alone. Main causes of morbidity and mortality: infections, bleeding, BMT complications, second malignancies. A: Far too low. B: Not without treatment. C: Too low. E: Not the main outcome.

questions.stem: What is the most common acquired bone marrow disorder in adults?
questions.explanation: MDS is the most common acquired BM disorder in adults: a clonal HSC disorder with cytopenia, ineffective hematopoiesis and progression to secondary AML in high-risk cases. A: Rare (2–4/million/year). B: Rare. C: Less common. D: Less common.

questions.stem: Physical damage, immune destruction and constitutional genetic defects can all cause aplastic anemia. What do they share?
questions.explanation: The three etiologies (physical/chemical damage, immune destruction, constitutional genetic defect) converge on a common pathology: an empty marrow. A: MDS. B: Myelofibrosis. C: Leukemia. E: Megaloblastic anemia.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old develops acute severe pancytopenia. The marrow is empty and fatty, and there is no drug, toxin or family history. What is the mechanism in most such cases?
questions.explanation: AA is immune in most severe and acute cases: T cell-mediated autoimmune destruction of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells. A: Antibodies cause single-lineage cytopenias. C: Parvovirus B19. D: Dyskeratosis congenita. E: Leukemia; marrow not empty.

questions.stem: Single-lineage peripheral cytopenias, such as autoimmune hemolytic anemia, are usually mediated by what?
questions.explanation: Single-cell peripheral cytopenias are antibody-mediated; aplastic anemia is T cell-mediated. B: Aplastic anemia. C: Dyskeratosis congenita. D: Fanconi anemia. E: PNH.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy recovers from acute hepatitis. Two months later he has bruising, fever and pancytopenia with an empty marrow. What is the most likely mechanism?

options.A: Direct infection of marrow progenitor cells
options.C: A T cell clone attacking liver and marrow

questions.explanation: Viral AA is mostly immune: T cell activation with cytokine release; an activated cytotoxic T cell clone recognizes similar target antigens on liver and marrow cells. Hepatitis and HIV are implicated in severe AA. A: Parvovirus B19. B: Marrow would be cellular. D: Marrow would not be empty. E: AA is T cell-mediated.

questions.stem: A child with sickle cell disease has a sudden fall in red cell production during parvovirus B19 infection. What is the mechanism?

options.C: Antibody-mediated lysis of mature red cells

questions.explanation: Most viral AA is immune-mediated, but parvovirus B19 infects progenitor cells directly. B: The mechanism of most viral AA. C: Hemolysis, not failed production. D: Not failed production. E: Not the viral mechanism.

questions.stem: A man develops aplastic anemia weeks after a course of chloramphenicol. His counts do not recover after the drug is stopped. What type of drug reaction is this?
questions.explanation: Drugs produce idiosyncratic and dose-dependent marrow suppression; idiosyncratic reactions (chloramphenicol) can leave irreversible AA. A: Predictable and reversible. B: Single-lineage cytopenias. C: Counts would recover. E: All lines are low.

questions.stem: A worker who has handled benzene solvents for years has severe pancytopenia and a fatty marrow. Which etiologic group fits?

options.A: T cell-mediated destruction of stem cells
options.E: Direct chemical injury to stem cells

questions.explanation: Direct injury to HSCs (physical and chemical damage): benzene, industrial chemicals, insecticides and pesticides can lead to severe AA. A: Immune AA. B: Inherited. C: Marrow would not be fatty. D: Marrow would be cellular.

questions.stem: How is marrow suppression from ionizing radiation best described?
questions.explanation: Ionizing radiation results in predictable, dose-dependent BM suppression. A: Chloramphenicol. C: Not radiation. D: Immune AA. E: Radiation affects all lines.

questions.stem: Years after immunosuppressive therapy for aplastic anemia, a 45-year-old has dark morning urine and hemolysis. Which disorder has most likely emerged?
questions.explanation: AA may coexist with or evolve into clonal disorders (PNH, MDS, AML, LGL), constitutional BMF syndromes or other autoimmune diseases. Dark urine with intravascular hemolysis = PNH. A: No hemolysis. B: Blasts, no hemoglobinuria. D: Splenomegaly, cytopenia. E: Inherited.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old has dark urine, abdominal vein thrombosis and Coombs-negative hemolysis with mild pancytopenia. Which gene is mutated?
questions.explanation: PNH: rare acquired HSPC disorder from a PIGA mutation → absence of the complement inhibitors CD59 and CD55; intravascular hemolysis, thrombosis, dark urine, end-organ dysfunction. A: Dyskeratosis congenita. B: Diamond-Blackfan anemia. C: Shwachman-Diamond syndrome. E: Congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia.

questions.stem: In PNH, the absence of which protein lets the membrane attack complex lyse red cells inside vessels?
questions.explanation: PNH red cells lack CD59 (which blocks intravascular hemolysis) and CD55 (which blocks extravascular hemolysis). A: Its loss allows extravascular hemolysis. B: Stem cell marker. D: β2 integrin; LAD. E: Platelet glycoprotein.

questions.stem: Which drug treats PNH by blocking complement?
questions.explanation: PNH treatment: anti-complement therapy (eculizumab). B: Thrombopoietin receptor agonist. C: Immunosuppression. D: Immunosuppression. E: Factor VIII mimetic.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old has pancytopenia. The marrow is hypercellular with dysplasia in all lineages, 8% blasts and ringed sideroblasts. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: MDS: hypercellular dysplastic marrow in all lineages with blasts (usually < 20%) and ringed sideroblasts. A: Hypocellular marrow. B: Blasts usually ≥ 20%. C: Hemolysis, no dysplasia. D: No dysplasia or blasts.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old has pancytopenia and a hypocellular marrow that also contains dysplastic cells. Which diagnosis shares features with aplastic anemia here?
questions.explanation: A subset of MDS patients (hypoplastic MDS) have a hypoplastic marrow that shares features with AA; it is in the AA differential. A: Normal or increased hematopoiesis. C: Cellular marrow. D: Fibrosis. E: LGL infiltration.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old with neutropenia and splenomegaly has many large lymphocytes with cytoplasmic granules infiltrating his blood and marrow. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: LGL leukemia: a clonal adult disease with cytopenia, splenomegaly and infiltration of blood and marrow by LGLs. B: No infiltration; no splenomegaly. C: Myeloid blasts. D: No clonal infiltration. E: Dysplasia, not LGLs.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old with pallor, gum bleeding and recurrent infections has pancytopenia with a low reticulocyte count. Which test establishes aplastic anemia?
questions.explanation: AA workup: clinical scenario, CBC (pancytopenia, low reticulocytes), then marrow aspirate and biopsies. A: Fanconi anemia. B: PNH. C: Megaloblastic anemia. D: Hypersplenism.

questions.stem: Which marrow biopsy finding fits aplastic anemia?
questions.explanation: AA marrow: hypocellular/aplastic with few HSPCs, empty fatty marrow, no malignant cells or fibrosis, CD34 cells almost completely absent. A: MDS. C: Myelofibrosis. D: Leukemia. E: Megaloblastic anemia.

questions.stem: In aplastic anemia, which marrow cells are almost completely absent?
questions.explanation: AA marrow: hypocellular, empty fatty marrow, CD34 (stem and progenitor) cells almost completely absent. A: Abundant. B: Not the defining loss. D: Not the defining loss. E: Not the defining loss.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old has aplastic anemia: marrow cellularity 15%, ANC 0.4, platelets 15, absolute reticulocytes 50 ×10⁹/L. How is it classified?
questions.explanation: SAA: marrow cellularity < 25% plus 2 of 3: ANC < 0.5, platelets < 20, ARC < 60 ×10⁹/L. All three are met; ANC is not below 0.2. A: Needs ANC < 0.2. B: SAA criteria are met. C: No dysplasia given. E: All lines are low.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old has aplastic anemia: marrow cellularity 10%, ANC 0.1, platelets 8, absolute reticulocytes 20 ×10⁹/L. How is it classified?
questions.explanation: VSAA: SAA criteria plus ANC < 0.2 ×10⁹/L. B: ANC < 0.2 upgrades it. C: SAA criteria are met. D: All lines are low. E: All lines are low.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old has aplastic anemia: marrow cellularity 20%, ANC 0.9, platelets 40, absolute reticulocytes 70 ×10⁹/L. How is it classified?
questions.explanation: NSAA: ≥ 2 cytopenias not fulfilling SAA or VSAA criteria. SAA needs 2 of ANC < 0.5, platelets < 20, ARC < 60 ×10⁹/L. A: None of the three blood criteria is met. B: ANC is not < 0.2. C: Marrow is hypocellular. D: Needs a cause and recovery.

questions.stem: For severe aplastic anemia, marrow cellularity must be below what value?
questions.explanation: SAA and VSAA: marrow cellularity < 25%. A: Listed for non-severe AA. C: Too low. D: Too high. E: Too high.

questions.stem: An 18-year-old with severe aplastic anemia has no dysmorphic features. Why is a chromosome breakage test still done before transplant?

options.C: An inherited syndrome may be hidden

questions.explanation: Patients with SAA can have an unrecognized inherited BMF syndrome because of phenotypic heterogeneity; the breakage test is done in AA at any age before HSCT. A: Needs a biopsy. B: Needs flow cytometry. D: Not its use. E: Not its use.

questions.stem: Besides disease severity and age, which factor most shapes the choice of treatment in severe aplastic anemia?
questions.explanation: Choice of treatment depends on disease severity, the patient's age, donor availability and access to optimal therapies. A: Not a listed factor. B: Not a listed factor. C: Not a listed factor. E: Part of severity.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old with severe aplastic anemia has an HLA-matched sibling. What is the first-line treatment?
questions.explanation: BMT is first-line therapy for SAA in children and young adults with a fully matched donor: high cure rate and sustained recovery, especially at a young age. B: For patients > 40 or without a donor. C: After inadequate IST response. D: Constitutional BMF. E: PNH.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old has newly diagnosed severe aplastic anemia. What is the first-line treatment?
questions.explanation: IST (anti-thymocyte globulin + cyclosporine): patients > 40 years with newly diagnosed SAA/VSAA, and younger patients without a matched sibling donor. A: IST is first above 40. B: Added after inadequate IST response. D: Constitutional BMF. E: PNH.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old with severe aplastic anemia has no matched sibling donor. Which treatment is indicated?
questions.explanation: IST is given to patients over 40 with new SAA/VSAA and to younger patients without a matched sibling donor. A: Hypersplenism. C: Constitutional BMF. D: PNH. E: Shwachman-Diamond syndrome.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old with severe aplastic anemia responds poorly to anti-thymocyte globulin and cyclosporine and is not a transplant candidate. Which drug is added?
questions.explanation: Eltrombopag: in newly diagnosed SAA/VSAA with inadequate response to IST who are not BMT candidates; higher response rate when combined with IST. A: PNH. B: For fever and neutropenia. C: Constitutional BMF. D: Hemophilia A.

questions.stem: On which receptor does eltrombopag act?
questions.explanation: Eltrombopag is a thrombopoietin receptor agonist. A: Not eltrombopag. B: Not eltrombopag. C: Platelet integrin. E: T cell receptor.

questions.stem: In matched sibling transplant for severe aplastic anemia, which age group has the best survival?
questions.explanation: Survival after first-line HLA-identical sibling BMT for SAA: ~86% at 1–20 years, 76% at 21–40 years, 55% over 40. B: About 76%. C: About 55%. D: Worse than younger patients. E: Worse than younger patients.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old with severe aplastic anemia awaiting transplant has received 40 red cell units, and his ferritin is very high. What should be added?
questions.explanation: Supportive care in AA: treatment and prophylaxis of infections, restrictive transfusions, iron chelation for iron overload, G-CSF in fever and neutropenia, withdrawal of the etiologic agent. A: For fever and neutropenia. B: PNH. C: Not indicated. D: Constitutional BMF.

questions.stem: Which transfusion approach is recommended in aplastic anemia?
questions.explanation: Supportive care includes restrictive transfusions (platelets and packed RBCs). A: Not restrictive. B: Not restrictive. C: Not restrictive. E: Not listed.

questions.stem: A man with aplastic anemia develops fever with an ANC of 0.2 ×10⁹/L. Besides antibiotics, which supportive drug is given?
questions.explanation: Supportive care: treatment and prophylaxis of infections, G-CSF in fever and neutropenia. A: Not for febrile neutropenia. B: PNH. D: Iron overload. E: Constitutional BMF.

questions.stem: A woman develops aplastic anemia weeks after starting an antiseizure drug. What is the first step?
questions.explanation: Antiseizure drugs can cause AA; supportive care includes withdrawal of the etiologic agent. A: PNH. C: Hypersplenism. D: Constitutional BMF. E: SDS.

questions.stem: Since the 1960s, survival in severe aplastic anemia has risen from about 30% to about 85%. Which change contributed?
questions.explanation: Survival improved with increasing availability of HSCT, more effective IST, targeted therapy and better supportive care. A: Not listed. B: Not listed. D: Transfusions are restrictive. E: PNH.

questions.stem: In a child with pancytopenia, which feature points most to an inherited marrow failure syndrome?

options.B: Early onset with a family history
options.E: A PNH clone on flow cytometry

questions.explanation: Inherited BMF clues: young age of onset, positive family history, chronicity, multi-organ involvement, high HbF and MCV. A: Acquired. C: Acquired. D: Malignancy. E: Acquired.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old with previously normal counts develops severe pancytopenia over 3 weeks. She has petechiae, no lymphadenopathy, no organomegaly and no dysmorphic features. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Sudden onset, often severe pancytopenia: acquired AA. Family history, early onset, chronicity or somatic findings: inherited. Lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly: malignancy. B: Early onset, somatic findings. C: Skin, nail and mouth signs. D: No splenomegaly. E: No nodes or organomegaly.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old with pancytopenia has generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. Which category does this suggest?
questions.explanation: Lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly with pancytopenia point to malignancy. A: No nodes or organomegaly. B: Early onset, somatic findings. C: Recovers on serial CBCs. D: Hemolysis, thrombosis.

questions.stem: Which coexisting disorder should be looked for in every adult with aplastic anemia?
questions.explanation: Adults: look for co-existent MDS, PNH and AML in all patients. A: Not related. B: Not related. C: Not related. E: Not related.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old with severe aplastic anemia fails to respond to immunosuppressive therapy. What should be done next in the workup?

options.D: Repeat serum ferritin and iron studies

questions.explanation: Adults: do genetic testing for inherited disorders and in non-responders to IST. A: PNH. B: Hypersplenism. C: SDS. D: Does not explain the failure.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old has newly diagnosed aplastic anemia and no dysmorphic features. Which test should be part of the workup?
questions.explanation: Children with AA need genetic testing to identify inherited abnormalities; the breakage test is done in AA at any age, before HSCT. A: LAD. C: Cystic fibrosis. D: Immune hemolysis. E: Hemoglobinopathies.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy of consanguineous parents has short stature, café-au-lait spots, an absent thumb, pancytopenia, a high MCV and raised HbF. Which test confirms the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Congenital abnormalities, short stature, pancytopenia and a positive chromosomal breakage test: Fanconi anemia. High HbF and MCV are clues to inherited BMF. B: Dyskeratosis congenita. C: Diamond-Blackfan anemia. D: Shwachman-Diamond syndrome. E: Congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia.

questions.stem: When Fanconi anemia cells are exposed to diepoxybutane or mitomycin C, what do they show?
questions.explanation: FA cells show chromosome breakage and radial formation when treated with DNA cross-linking agents (DEB or mitomycin C) and harvested in metaphase. A: Dyskeratosis congenita. B: MDS. D: PNH. E: Chediak-Higashi syndrome.

questions.stem: Fanconi anemia results from a defect in which cellular process?
questions.explanation: Fanconi anemia is a DNA repair disease: mutations in FA genes coding for proteins of a DNA repair pathway, with cellular sensitivity to DNA-damaging agents. A: Dyskeratosis congenita. B: SDS and DBA. C: CAT. E: PNH.

questions.stem: What is the inheritance of Fanconi anemia?
questions.explanation: FA is autosomal recessive (23 FA genes; carrier frequency 1/200–300). A: Most DBA. B: Most severe DC. C: Not described. D: Not described.

questions.stem: What is the most common inherited bone marrow failure syndrome?
questions.explanation: Fanconi anemia is the most common IBMFS; it generally manifests between 3 and 12 years, and many patients do not reach adulthood. A: 2–5% of IBMF. C: Rare. D: Single lineage. E: Rare.

questions.stem: Which physical finding is the most frequent in Fanconi anemia?
questions.explanation: PE findings in FA: skin pigmentation 60%, short stature 57%, upper limb abnormality 48%, head/microcephaly 27%, renal 23%, developmental delay 13%, none reported 20%. B: 57%. C: 48%. D: 27%. E: 23%.

questions.stem: About what share of patients with Fanconi anemia have no reported physical abnormality?
questions.explanation: In about 20% of FA patients no abnormality is reported, so a normal exam does not exclude FA. A: Too low. B: Too high. C: Skin pigmentation. E: Developmental delay.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy has reticulated skin pigmentation, dystrophic nails, oral leukoplakia and progressive pancytopenia. Which test supports the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Dyskeratosis congenita (telomere biology disease): skin pigmentation, nail dystrophy and oral leukoplakia, with cancer predisposition; short telomeres and DKC1 mutations confirm it. A: Fanconi anemia. B: Diamond-Blackfan anemia. D: Shwachman-Diamond syndrome. E: PNH.

questions.stem: A boy has the most severe, X-linked form of dyskeratosis congenita. Which gene is mutated?
questions.explanation: DC is genetically heterogeneous (telomerase and shelterin genes): X-linked recessive DKC1 (most severe), autosomal dominant telomerase RNA gene, and autosomal recessive forms. A: Diamond-Blackfan anemia. B: Shwachman-Diamond syndrome. C: TAR. D: PNH.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old with dyskeratosis congenita and severe marrow failure is considered for stem cell transplant. What is the main concern?
questions.explanation: SCT is not recommended in DC because of the high risk of interstitial pulmonary disease. A: PNH. B: SDS. D: TAR. E: Chediak-Higashi syndrome.

questions.stem: What is the commonest cause of death in dyskeratosis congenita?
questions.explanation: In DC, BMF is seen in 85% and is the commonest cause of mortality. B: Another manifestation. C: Another manifestation. D: A predisposition. E: Cellular immune deficiency is less common.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old has greasy stools, failure to thrive, recurrent severe infections, short stature and neutropenia. Fecal elastase is low. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: SDS: rare AR disorder with pancreatic insufficiency (low trypsinogen, amylase, fecal elastase), BMF (neutropenia most common), short stature and increased AML/MDS risk. A: No neutropenia. B: No pancreatic insufficiency. C: Isolated anemia. E: Isolated anemia.

questions.stem: Mutations in the SBDS gene impair which process?
questions.explanation: The SBDS gene encodes proteins implicated in ribosome biogenesis. A: Fanconi anemia. C: Dyskeratosis congenita. D: CAT. E: Chediak-Higashi syndrome.

questions.stem: Which treatment is specific to Shwachman-Diamond syndrome among the inherited marrow failure syndromes?
questions.explanation: IBMFS treatment: supportive care (infections, restrictive transfusions, iron chelation, G-CSF), pancreatic enzyme replacement in SDS, androgens, splenectomy/cholecystectomy in CDA. A: CDA. B: CDA. C: PNH. E: Any transfused patient.

questions.stem: A newborn has petechiae, platelets of 15 ×10⁹/L and absent megakaryocytes in the marrow, with no limb or other birth defects. Which gene is most likely mutated?
questions.explanation: Congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia: early thrombocytopenia with absent/reduced megakaryocytes from MPL (thrombopoietin receptor) mutations; no birth defects; may evolve to AA, MDS or AML. A: TAR; absent radii. C: Diamond-Blackfan anemia. D: Shwachman-Diamond syndrome. E: Dyskeratosis congenita.

questions.stem: A newborn has platelets of 20 ×10⁹/L, short forearms with absent radii and a heart defect. Which gene is most likely affected?
questions.explanation: TAR: AR disorder of the RBM8A gene (1q21.1): early thrombocytopenia, absent radii, cardiac, skeletal and urogenital anomalies; uncertain cancer predisposition. A: CAT; no birth defects. B: Diamond-Blackfan anemia. C: Shwachman-Diamond syndrome. D: Dyskeratosis congenita.

questions.stem: A 3-month-old has Hb 5 g/dL with a high MCV, reticulocytes near zero, normal WBC and platelets, and a thumb anomaly. Which finding supports the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Diamond-Blackfan anemia: early pure red cell aplasia with congenital anomalies; isolated macrocytic anemia, reticulocytopenia, few erythroid precursors, increased HbF and red cell ADA activity. B: Fanconi anemia. C: Dyskeratosis congenita. D: Shwachman-Diamond syndrome. E: CAT and TAR.

questions.stem: Diamond-Blackfan anemia most often results from a mutation in which gene?
questions.explanation: DBA (mostly autosomal dominant) is due to mutations in ribosomal protein genes, RPS19 most often. A: Dyskeratosis congenita. B: Shwachman-Diamond syndrome. D: CAT. E: TAR.

questions.stem: In Diamond-Blackfan anemia, what does the bone marrow show?
questions.explanation: DBA: early onset pure red cell aplasia from failure of erythropoiesis; marked decrease of erythroid precursors in the marrow. A: CAT and TAR. B: SCN. C: Aplastic anemia. D: MDS.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old has lifelong anemia, jaundice, gallstones, splenomegaly and iron overload. Marrow erythroblasts show nuclear abnormalities. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: CDA: rare hereditary dyserythropoiesis with ineffective erythropoiesis; anemia, jaundice, cholelithiasis, splenomegaly, iron overload; diagnosis by erythroblast nuclear abnormalities in the marrow and CDA genotyping. B: Few erythroid precursors. C: Normal erythroblasts. D: Acquired. E: Neutropenia, pancreatic insufficiency.

questions.stem: Which inherited marrow failure syndrome may need splenectomy or cholecystectomy?
questions.explanation: Splenectomy/cholecystectomy is used in CDA (jaundice, splenomegaly, gallstones). A: Not listed. B: Not listed. D: Not listed. E: Pancreatic enzymes.

questions.stem: Which inherited marrow failure syndrome causes isolated neutropenia?
questions.explanation: SCN: isolated neutropenia, maturation arrest at the promyelocyte–myelocyte stage, predisposition to leukemia; G-CSF, SCT. A: Pancreatic insufficiency too. B: Isolated anemia. C: Thrombocytopenia. E: Thrombocytopenia.

questions.stem: An 11-year-old with Fanconi anemia has worsening cytopenias and no matched donor. Which drug may improve his counts?
questions.explanation: Androgens are used in IBMFS; constitutional BMF is treated with sex hormones or BMT, immune AA with IST, BMT or eltrombopag. A: PNH. C: Immune AA. D: SDS. E: Hemophilia A.

questions.stem: After a successful stem cell transplant for Fanconi anemia, a 15-year-old's counts are normal. What remains?
questions.explanation: SCT is curative in 60–90% but treats only the cytopenia; it does not decrease early-onset malignancy. Monitor for organ dysfunction and cancer. A: Cytopenia is cured. B: Curative in 60–90%. C: SDS. D: PNH.

questions.stem: Which type of bone marrow failure is usually self-limiting?
questions.explanation: Prognosis by cause: inherited = lifelong cytopenia and higher cancer risk; acquired = short course but can be permanent and life-threatening; viral-associated = usually self-limiting. A: Lifelong cytopenia. B: Mortality > 70% untreated. D: Lifelong cytopenia. E: Clonal; can progress.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old with pancytopenia has teardrop cells and nucleated red cells on the smear. What does this favor over aplastic anemia?
questions.explanation: Infiltrative marrow disease (malignancies, primary myelofibrosis, TB, fungi, storage cells) is told from AA by smear changes (blasts, schistocytes, teardrops) and marrow morphologic, cytogenetic or molecular abnormalities. B: No smear changes. C: No teardrops. D: No teardrops. E: Hemolysis, thrombosis.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old strict vegan has pancytopenia, MCV 118 fL, hypersegmented neutrophils, high LDH and high indirect bilirubin. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Megaloblastic anemia (B12 and/or folate deficiency): pancytopenia with ineffective erythropoiesis; oval macrocytes, hypersegmented neutrophils, high LDH and indirect bilirubin. A: No hemolysis markers. B: No hypersegmentation or high LDH. C: No splenomegaly given. E: Infancy; isolated anemia.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old has pancytopenia 1 week after an acute viral illness. Serial CBCs improve over the next 2 weeks. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Transient BM suppression: chemotherapy, radiation, overwhelming sepsis or acute viral infection; predictable; serial CBCs show improvement in days to weeks. A: Would not recover alone. C: Lifelong. D: Would not recover. E: Needs splenomegaly.

questions.stem: A man with liver cirrhosis and a large spleen has mild pancytopenia. The marrow shows normal to increased hematopoiesis. What is the cause?
questions.explanation: Hypersplenism: cytopenia due to splenomegaly (cirrhosis, portal vein thrombosis, infiltration, hemoglobinopathies); milder than infiltrative disease; normal or increased marrow hematopoiesis. A: Marrow would be empty. B: Abnormal marrow; more severe cytopenia. C: Megaloblastic marrow. E: Dysplastic marrow.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old with aplastic anemia has a PNH clone of 5% on flow cytometry. What does this finding favor?
questions.explanation: Acquired BMF: PNH positive (> 1%) in 30–50%; constitutional BMF is PNH negative. B: PNH-negative. C: PNH-negative. D: PNH-negative. E: PNH-negative.
